Contrasting Light Transmission in Different Arctic Sea Ice Regimes During Summer
candidates.abstract: Sea ice optical properties regulate the transfer of solar radiation into the Arctic Ocean, influencing upper-ocean heating, sea ice melt, and biological productivity. However, observations comparing the seasonal evolution of under-ice light fields across different Arctic sea ice regimes remain scarce. Here, we present repeated remotely operated vehicle surveys conducted during the 2025 CONTRASTS expedition over three representative Arctic sea ice regimes: seasonal first-year ice, mixed first- and second-year ice, and older, thicker ice. Eleven surveys in July and August combined broadband transmittance, ice draft, autonomous radiation stations, and spatial statistics to quantify the magnitude, variability, and seasonal evolution of light transmission and its contribution to the upper-ocean energy budget. Mean transmittance differed substantially among regimes, reaching up to 21% beneath first-year ice but only 12% and 6% beneath second-year and multiyear ice, respectively. While first-year ice exhibited the highest initial transmittance, snowfall reduced it by 40%, whereas second-year ice nearly doubled its transmittance during summer. In contrast, multiyear ice remained opaque despite gradual thinning. Spatial analyses revealed characteristic patch sizes of tens of meters associated with melt ponds, highlighting the heterogeneity of the under-ice light field. Solar radiation transmitted through sea ice and absorbed in open water ranged from 7 to 25W/m 2 , accounting for 30-47% of the melt-equivalent basal heat flux. Altogether, these results demonstrate that sea ice regime strongly controls both the magnitude and seasonal evolution of radiative energy transfer into the Arctic Ocean and should be explicitly represented in studies of sea ice melt and upper-ocean ecosystems.

candidates.title: Electrically switchable liquid crystal lens for bright-field and spiral phase contrast imaging
candidates.abstract: Bright-field imaging and phase contrast imaging, as two of the most representative modes in optical imaging, play significant roles in microscopy and optical analog computing, providing complementary and comprehensive morphological information of target objects. The development of devices capable of switching between or simultaneously performing these two modes has become a research focus. However, existing dual-mode imaging devices often suffer from insufficient integration, inflexible switching, and complex fabrication processes. Here, an electrically switchable dual-functional liquid crystal (LC) lens architecture based on laser direct writing is presented. One demonstration of the dual-mode LC lens (DM-LCL) consists of two vertically stacked lenses: a focusing lens for bright-field imaging and a spiral lens for spiral phase contrast imaging. By varying the applied voltage, different lens phase functions can be activated, enabling distinct imaging modes. The fabricated DM-LCL produces focused light fields consistent with theoretical simulations. Additionally, the optical and imaging performance across multiple wavelengths has been experimentally validated. Furthermore, an electrically switchable varifocal LC lens capable of simultaneous dual-mode imaging within the same field of view is demonstrated, validating the adaptability of the proposed architecture. The proposed LC lens exhibits switching speeds on the order of tens of milliseconds. This architecture provides a reliable solution for ultra-compact, fast-switching dual-mode imaging components and enables real-time adaptive imaging, showing significant potential for applications in microscopy, optical analog computing, and biomedicine.

candidates.title: Depth-selective autofocus technology for multi-layer interfaces based on pupil-plane spatial light field modulation
candidates.abstract: To address signal overlapping and false focusing in multi-layer reflective interfaces, an integrated autofocus (AF) system is presented. Firstly, an adjustable off-axis aperture utilizes eccentric masking to physically isolate reflected spots from varying depths, minimizing signal crosstalk. Subsequently, a low-complexity algorithm for spot extraction and centroid localization is implemented using first-order forward difference scanning. This algorithm incorporates a dual-decision logic based on a cumulative drop-depth threshold and an amplitude-width integral model to accurately extract target spots amidst lead-in noise and periodic clutter. Experimental results on 0.2mm SiC and 0.17mm SiO<sub>2</sub> samples demonstrate reliable surface recognition within a ±150 μm defocus range, achieving a measurement error within ±5 μm and a 75Hz output frequency. Highly compatible with FPGA implementation, this solution provides a high-precision, real-time closed-loop focusing method for high-throughput industrial inspection.

candidates.title: Light-Field-to-Bits Computing via an Online-Trainable Cascaded Optoelectronic Neural Network
candidates.abstract: Abstract Optical computing encodes and processes information through the continuous evolution of optical fields, whereas digital electronic systems operate on discrete logical states. Conventional optical-to-electronic interfaces convert measured optical responses into electronically accessible data, with task-specific interpretation subsequently performed in the electronic domain. Here, we introduce and experimentally validate a proof-of-concept light-field-to-bits (LFB) computing architecture that maps information-bearing light fields onto predefined 4-bit codewords. The proposed architecture comprises two cascaded diffractive layers that route optical energy at the output plane into eight predefined regions of interest (ROIs) arranged as four differential pairs, with each pair encoding one bit through relative-intensity comparison. We physically implement the first diffractive layer and computationally emulate the second, using a CMOS sensor to capture the intermediate intensity distribution. We further develop a differentiable physics-assisted surrogate model within a camera-in-the-loop framework. The experimental prototype achieves 4-bit codeword accuracies of 95.31% for geometrically perturbed hexadecimal inputs and 93.36% for traffic-sign inputs subjected to combined viewpoint distortion and noise. Meanwhile, the optical front-end exploits the intrinsic parallelism of diffractive propagation, performing high-dimensional optical transformations equivalent to ∼51.2 Giga-Operations (GOPs) of multiply accumulate (MAC) operations within a ∼1.16 ns optical time-of-flight, while the electronic stage only performs lightweight spatial aggregation at the scale of tens of Mega-FLOPs. This strategy establishes the feasibility of LFB computing as an interface between continuous optical information processing and discrete digital decision-making for latency-sensitive machine vision and edge sensing.

candidates.title: Two-module upgrade for 3D, high-resolution microscopy DMD patterned excitation and light-field detection
candidates.abstract: We present a modular upgrade to conventional widefield microscopy that integrates Fourier light field microscopy (FLFM) with structured illumination microscopy (SIM) for high-resolution volumetric biological imaging. The system combines a digital micromirror device (DMD)-based patterned illumination module with a light field detection path added to a commercial microscope, enabling flexible switching between widefield and FLFM modalities. By incorporating both analytical (MAP-SIM) and machine-learning-based (ML-SIM) reconstruction methods, we demonstrate significant resolution enhancement and background suppression in both 2D and 3D imaging. Experimental validation on murine intestinal organoids shows that applying SIM prior to FLFM reconstruction yields up to 1.4× lateral resolution improvement while preserving volumetric information. Additionally, FLFM acquisition drastically reduces photobleaching compared to conventional z-stack imaging. The proposed setup provides a cost-effective and versatile platform for multi-color, 3D imaging, with potential applications in microscopy education, or live-cell imaging.

candidates.title: Non-uniformly sampled aperture-coded light-field microscopy
candidates.abstract: Light-field microscopy enables three-dimensional volumetric imaging without mechanical scanning, making it highly promising for biomedical research. Conventional microlens-array-based light-field microscopes capture the light-field in a single snapshot but suffer from a trade-off between angular and spatial resolution, which limits spatial resolution. Aperture-coded light-field microscopy achieves full-resolution spatial sampling yet requires multiple measurements, thereby compromising temporal resolution. To overcome this limitation, we propose a non-uniformly sampled aperture-coded light-field microscopy method that exploits the non-uniform energy distribution in the aperture (Fourier) plane. Specifically, dense sampling is applied in the central region and sparse sampling toward the periphery. A single-pixel imaging algorithm is then used to reconstruct the 4D light-field. Experimental results show that our method reduces the number of required encodings by more than half compared to uniformly sampled methods while maintaining high image fidelity within a limited refocusing range. This facilitates the practical adoption of aperture-coded light-field microscopy.

candidates.title: Multi-scale cost aggregation with view interaction and edge constraints for light field disparity estimation
candidates.abstract: Light-field cameras can simultaneously capture spatial and angular information of a scene, providing a rich data foundation for applications such as 3D reconstruction, refocusing, and light-field reconstruction. As a key step in recovering the geometric structure of light-field scenes, disparity estimation play a crucial role in determining the performance of downstream applications. However, existing light-field disparity estimation methods often suffer from high computational complexity and low inference efficiency. To address these issues, this paper proposes a lightweight end-to-end light-field disparity estimation network based on multi-scale cost aggregation with view interaction and edge constraints. Specifically, the proposed network takes the central view as the reference and constructs multi-scale cost volumes by modeling the interaction relationships between adjacent corresponding views around the reference view, thereby enabling efficient disparity estimation. In addition, an edge constraint sub-network is introduced to impose structural constraints on the edge information of the reference view and refine disparity boundary regions generated through view interaction, effectively suppressing over-smoothing and enhancing the representation of fine structural details. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed network achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art light-field disparity estimation methods while significantly reducing computational costs and improving efficiency.

candidates.title: Wide-viewing-angle 3D light-field display based on a single-layer patterned microlens array
candidates.abstract: Light-field three-dimensional (3D) display can modulate both the intensity and direction of light rays, but conventional devices usually require precise alignment between the lens array and elemental pattern array, and their viewing angle is limited by the elemental aperture and focal length. To realize a compact wide-viewing-angle 3D display, we propose a single-layer patterned microlens array with a position-dependent curved phase. The pattern information, local focusing phase, and global curved phase are integrated into one microstructured layer. In this design, the local focusing phase reconstructs the elemental light field, whereas the curved phase redirects the chief rays of different microlens elements in a manner similar to a virtual large-aperture lens. Wave-optics simulations show that the curved phase introduces position-dependent chief-ray deflection and expands the effective viewing zone. Experiments show that the vertical full viewing angle is approximately 24° without the curved phase and is extended to approximately 32° and 52° after introducing virtual lens phases with focal lengths of 120 mm and 60 mm, respectively.

candidates.title: Predictive modeling of speckle field statistics in phase-change disorder metasurfaces
candidates.abstract: A disordered metasurface, unlike an ordered metasurface, lacks symmetry and has random terms in terms of shape, size, and position arrangement. Phase change materials (PCMs) provide dynamic reconfigurability and, when combined with disordered metasurfaces, create a smart, tunable surface that controls the optical response in a random or engineered-disorder manner. Although the deterministic control of wavefronts using programmable order metasurfaces has advanced considerably, predictive theories that link structural disorder and phase transitions to the statistical properties of speckle fields remain challenging. In this work, we present a predictive framework for speckle fields in PCM-based disordered metasurfaces that integrates analytical modeling. For a 25μm× 25μm size at a 1550nm wavelength, the model predicts the intensity probability density, contrast, entropy, spatial correlation, and field. The work shows that there is a low correlation of patterns after phase switching from one state to another state, and also high entropy. These geometry-dependent changes in the optical response in terms of transmission amplitude and phase substantially reorganize the spatial speckle distribution. This phase switching preserves the characteristic speckle scale while generating strongly distinguishable spatial intensity patterns. These simulation results show the potential of nonvolatile Ge<sub>2</sub>Sb<sub>2</sub>Se<sub>4</sub>Te<sub>1</sub> (GSST) geometry-dependent disordered metasurfaces for reconfigurable statistical light-field encoding, optical authentication, and physical unclonable-function (PUF) applications.

Light Field Optimization for Negative Features in Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing
candidates.abstract: Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing (tVAM) has gained popularity for 3D fabrication of complex structures for tissue engineering and biofabrication. Unlike other methods of additive manufacturing which sequentially build parts layer-by-layer, tVAM delivers light energy into photocurable resins using computed light intensity fields (LIFs) to cure entire 3D regions at once, making patterning of soft or biocompatible materials possible. Such materials are ubiquitous in organ-on-chip and tissue engineering applications, where vascularization is foundational to providing effective nutrient supply and waste removal. Intentional 3D patterning of vasculature, or similar channel structures, what we term ”negative geometries”, is a unique challenge in tVAM. This study is the first systematic investigation of negative feature fabrication in tVAM. We show that optimization algorithms made for positive geometries yield poor results when implemented on negative geometries. We then propose two simple algorithmic modifications to improve the optimization of LIFs for negative geometries. We investigate the usable bounds of these approaches and show significant improvement in the ability to resolve negative features in 2D test coupons as well as full 3D structures. The ability to resolve negative features in tVAM-printed parts expands the value of this fabrication technique in lab-on-a-chip and biofabrication applications.

candidates.title: Towards multiphysics 4D particle tracking in microchannels with high-speed light-field microscopy
candidates.abstract: This work presents recent progress toward high-resolution, single-camera 4D particle tracking in microfluidic environments using a custom-built Fourier light-field microscope. The system captures seven angular views on a single high-speed sensor and reconstructs volumetric particle motion without requiring multiple synchronized cameras. Building on previous work that demonstrated particle localization accuracy below 0.3 micrometers, the present study extends the measurement depth from about 50 micrometers to more than 160 micrometers by using experimentally registered defocused point spread functions and neural-network-based particle detection. The microscope maintains a 370 micrometer wide field of view and records at 1300 frames per second streamed directly to disk. The improved framework is demonstrated in several challenging microfluidic configurations, including pillar wakes, junction flows, and a backward-facing step geometry from the first defocused particle tracking challenge. These results show that high-speed Fourier light-field microscopy can provide compact, single-camera access to time-resolved 3D flow measurements in optically constrained microchannels. Future developments will extend the method beyond seeded-particle velocimetry toward multiphysics measurements involving near-wall transport, scalar fields, biofilms, active microswimmers, and intensity-based reconstructions.

candidates.title: Transient Three-Dimensional Measurement of Ice Crystal Accretion Using a Plenoptic Camera
candidates.abstract: Monitoring the three-dimensional formation of ice layers on airfoils during icing wind tunnel experiments is extremely challenging. For the first time, this paper demonstrates the use of a single plenoptic camera to perform transient, nonintrusive in situ measurements of ice crystal accretion. Experiments have been conducted in the Altitude Icing Wind Tunnel at the National Research Council of Canada under different icing conditions to assess the potential of the new technique. Using the camera in a close-up configuration, the results show the evolution of the three-dimensional shape of the accreted ice in high spatial and temporal resolution and in absolute metric units. The computed surface meshes allow for a detailed analysis in terms of ice shape, surface area, and ice volume. Posttest shapes are compared to measurements taken using a commercial laser scanner. Although not rated for ice surfaces, this device is used as a reference to compare the detailed surface structure after registering the data sets. The results of the two methods are in good agreement and show a mean relative deviation of the plenoptic camera of about 0.15 mm.

candidates.title: Information in correlation detection for plenoptic imaging purposes
candidates.abstract: In the present work, we quantify the information content of intensity correlation measurements as compared to conventional intensity detection. In particular, we focus on the problem of estimating the separation between two point-like emitters and evaluate Fisher information for the two types of measurements. We consider two different scenarios: intensity correlations are measured, in the first case, in the image plane, and, in the second case, between the image and the Fourier plane of the object. Both detection schemes are shown to benefit from measuring correlations between the detected intensities, a result that indicates the advantages offered by both quantum and quantum-inspired (i.e., correlation-based) imaging protocols over conventional, intensity based, approaches.

Development of Plenoptic Camera as Wavefront Sensor
candidates.abstract: The accuracy of a signal decreases with an increase in distance and turbulence level in the fields of remote sensing ,freespaceopticalcommunication, and directed energy applications. Due to the optical effects in turbulent atmospheric conditions for distances beyond the range of a kilometre, weak energy signals limit the range for these applications. The optical effect arises from the variation in temperature and causes fluctuations in the refractive index of air. These weak signals have distorted phase and amplitude, which is corrected using adaptive optics. Adaptive optics uses a wavefront sensor to detect and compensate the distortion effects. The development of the plenoptic camera as a wavefront sensor is a significant development in the field of adaptive optics. A plenoptic camera is capable of wavefront sensing and its post image processing algorithms are used for image correction, phase and amplitude corrections, and decoding optical signals. In this paper, we develop a plenoptic camera as an alternative to the wavefront sensor for strong atmospheric turbulence effects and compare its performance with the Shark-Hartmann wavefrontsensor.Thedesignedplenopticcameraisillustratedtoimproveoverthedrawbackofaconventional wavefront sensor that works well only at weak atmospheric turbulent conditions. Our results prove that the designed plenoptic camera can compensate to the effects of turbulence.

Dynamic modulation method for super-resolution wavefront reconstruction of a plenoptic sensor
candidates.abstract: Plenoptic sensors have found applications in wavefront detection in strong-turbulence environments, owing to their broad field-of-view and reduced susceptibility to phase aliasing. Nevertheless, their step-type slope response characteristics pose a limitation to further enhancing wavefront detection accuracy. In this paper, we introduce a new dynamic modulation method to our knowledge. This method enables the sensor to acquire multiple full-spectral images with distinct tilt modulations and subsequently fuse them into a single super-resolution plenoptic image. Both simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method substantially improves the accuracy of wavefront reconstruction when compared to other algorithms. The method proves effective for both point and extended targets and holds great promise for applications in fields such as astronomical observation, laser transmission, and computational imaging.

A Blur Feature-Guided Cascaded Calibration Method for Plenoptic Cameras
candidates.abstract: Accurate and robust calibration of multifocal plenoptic cameras is essential for high-precision 3D light field reconstruction. In this work, we propose a blur feature-guided cascaded calibration for the plenoptic camera. First, white images at different aperture values are used to estimate the high-confidence center point and radius of micro-images, and the defocus theory is used to estimate the initial values of the intrinsic parameters. Second, the gradient value is introduced to quantify the degree of blurring of the corner points, which are then divided into three types: clear, semi-clear, and blurred. Furthermore, a joint geometric constraint model of epipolar lines and virtual depth is constructed, and the coordinates of the semi-clear and blurred corner points are optimized in a step-by-step manner by using the clear corner point coordinates. The micro-image center ray projection equation is then devised to assist in the optimization of the microlens array core parameters and establish blur-adaptive credibility weights, thereby constructing a global nonlinear optimization. Finally, the proposed method is tested on both simulated and captured datasets, and the results exhibit superior performance when compared with the established methods described by Labussière, Nousias, and Liu. The proposed method excels in corner feature extraction, calibration accuracy of both internal and external parameters, and calibration sensitivity when applied to multifocal-length light field cameras, highlighting its advantages and robustness.

candidates.title: Plenoptic wavefront sensor reconstruction algorithm tailored for sensing turbulence
candidates.abstract: We present a plenoptic wavefront sensor algorithm adapted for the recovery of turbulent wavefronts. Our approach employs a specialized consolidation technique for incoherently combining phase tilt contributions from the individual cells of the composite sensor image. Using a synthetic turbulent wavefront and a numerical model of the plenoptic wavefront sensor to emulate the measurement process, we demonstrate the efficacy of our technique by reconstructing the turbulent wavefront from the composite sensor image and evaluating the sensor’s overall performance. We identify the sources of error intrinsic to the sensor architecture and discuss prospects for improving its performance.

Plenoptic self-aligned focusing schlieren
candidates.abstract: Abstract A plenoptic camera was coupled into a self-aligned focusing schlieren (SAFS) system, allowing for the instantaneous capture of focused schlieren images at multiple planes from a single snapshot. Each focused schlieren image can be refocused to an arbitrary depth, within limits discussed herein, revealing density gradients at different spatial locations in the flow. A description of the plenoptic SAFS system is presented, along with a characterization of the experimental system. This characterization details the two depths-of-field associated with a plenoptic camera; the so-called reduced aperture depth-of-field, which gives the refocusing range, and the full aperture depth-of-field, which determines the depth-of-field of the final refocused image. Further, the spatial resolution of the plenoptic SAFS system was determined via a modulation transfer function analysis using a slant-edge target. Finally, results of an experiment consisting of two helium jets in both side-by-side and inline, vertically-opposed configurations are presented, as well as results from a wind tunnel experiment.

candidates.title: An ultrafast plenoptic-camera system for high-resolution 3D particle tracking in unsegmented scintillators
candidates.abstract: Abstract Neutrino detectors, particle calorimeters and some dark matter detectors require dense and massive active materials. An extremely fine segmentation is desirable to achieve precise three-dimensional particle tracking. However, such systems introduce significant challenges in construction and demand a large number of readout electronics channels, leading to extremely high costs. In this article, we propose an alternative approach to elementary particle detection that enables ultrafast three-dimensional high-resolution imaging in large volumes of unsegmented scintillator. Enabling technologies are plenoptic systems and time-resolving single-photon avalanche diode array imaging sensors. Together, they enabled us, using a plenoptic camera, to reconstruct the origin of single photons in the scintillator. A case study focused on neutrino detection demonstrates full event reconstruction with a spatial resolution of two hundred micrometres. This work paves the way for a class of particle detectors whose capabilities should be further enhanced through future developments and expanded to Cherenkov light detection, medical imaging and neutron detection.

candidates.title: Experimental three-dimensional study of the atomization of multiple gas-assisted liquidjets with a single plenoptic camera
candidates.abstract: This work focuses on the performance of a plenoptic imaging setup for characterizing the three-dimensional properties of sprays produced by four air-assisted liquid jets in "fiber" atomization mode. This technique provides access to the 3D position and size of the droplets formed during atomization, over a depth of measurement larger than the field of view. The size distribution obtained by light field imaging agrees with those obtained by conventional imaging under the same flow conditions. The spatial distribution of the droplets shows very good agreement with the actual positions of the injection axes, which validates the plenoptic metrology. This metrology also provides access to the spatial distributions of key quantities such as drop concentration, interface area density and liquid volume fraction, whose 3D distributions are generally only accessible through numerical simulation.

candidates.title: Calculation and correction of response curves for wavefront sensing of extended targets using a plenoptic sensor
GenPIE: A Time-Resolved Plenoptic Imager
candidates.abstract: Capturing the full plenoptic light transport across spatial, angular, and temporal dimensions has long been a pursuit in computational imaging, yet it remains fundamentally constrained by the high dimensionality of the sampling space and the physical inaccessibility of scene regions due to self-occlusions. While time-resolved imaging records the temporal axis, existing methods are bottlenecked by the combinatorial complexity of the plenoptic function. This high dimensionality makes dense omni-dimensional sampling physically prohibitive. Simultaneously, tight coupling between illumination and viewpoint in current systems also precludes the full acquisition of plenoptic light transport. In this work, we present GenPIE, a Generative Plenoptic Imager designed to bridge the gap between sparse physical observations and high-dimensional light transport. We introduce a decoupled laser-detector hardware setup that enables independent control over illumination and detection, allowing for active probing of indirect light paths. To overcome the ill-posedness of sparse sampling and physical blind spots, we propose a generative inverse transient rendering framework. Our approach leverages 3D foundation models to provide strong semantic and 3D geometric priors for initialization, which are subsequently refined through a differentiable transient path tracer to ensure physically grounded adherence to the Transient Rendering Equation. We demonstrate that GenPIE supports a range of applications that are challenging for steady-state or purely neural methods, including disentangling multi-bounce light transport directly from captured transient videos, time unwarping, and time-resolved relighting. The project page is at https://wangzh1.github.io/GenPIE.

candidates.title: KPI‐NeRF: Hyperspectral Neural Radiance Fields from a Single Kaleidoscopic Plenoptic Image
candidates.abstract: Abstract Plenoptic imaging has excessive sampling requirements associated with the high dimensionality of the desired data. At the same time, this data is characterized by a high redundancy since images, in general, do not drastically change when changing the view point or when moving to neighbouring spectral channels. It is therefore desirable to interpolate data across viewpoints or spectral channels, exploiting this redundancy. In practice, a convenient way to acquire plenoptic data is via snapshot hyperspectral light field imaging. Such data can be obtained by individually spectrally filtering particular slices of the light field, e.g. individual light field views in the case of Kaleidoscopic Plenoptic Imaging (KPI) [MRK*13], or individual lenslet images in traditional light field cameras. In this work, we focus on Kaleidoscopic Plenoptic Imaging because of the simple optical modification that enables hyperspectral imaging: attaching a macroscopic broadband spectral filter array close to the sensor to acquire differently spectrally filtered light field subviews. The main computational challenge associated with this configuration is the registration of the spectrally filtered light field subviews to enable an interpolation of the data followed by spectral demultiplexing for every light field pixel. The underlying problem is the motion parallax between the light field views caused by the varying scene depth, an estimate of which is needed to register the subviews. However, classical intensity‐based registration fails in the case of spectrally pre‐filtered subviews. We therefore resort to an implicit scene representation using a newly developed NeRF variant that enables quantitatively correct spectral light field interpolation. Technically, we introduce a subspace‐representation of the desired scene spectra and estimate their coefficients using a NeRF modification. We successfully decode up to 29 spectral channels for lab and outdoor scenes. Additionally, we present an application of our technique to time‐sequences of snapshot images to acquire full plenoptic data. The temporal consistency is reasonable even though no special attempts at enforcing temporal coherence are made.
